entries.title: 🐍 Python basics - syntax overview
entries.content:
Python uses indentation (4 spaces) instead of braces.

```
# Variables
x = 10
name = "hello"
is_cool = True

# If / elif / else
if x > 5:
    print("big")
elif x == 5:
    print("five")
else:
    print("small")

# For loop
for i in range(5):      # 0 1 2 3 4
    print(i)

# While loop
while x > 0:
    x -= 1
```
tips: Indentation IS the syntax - mixing tabs and spaces causes errors
range(1, 21) gives 1 through 20 inclusive
Use f-strings for formatting: f"value is {x}"

entries.title: 📋 Lists - the Python workhorse
entries.content:
Lists are ordered, mutable, and can hold anything.

```
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
nums.append(6)       # [1,2,3,4,5,6]
nums.pop()           # removes last: [1,2,3,4,5]
nums[0]              # 1  (indexing)
nums[-1]             # 5  (last element)
nums[1:3]            # [2, 3]  (slicing)
nums[::-1]           # reversed copy
len(nums)            # 5
```

List comprehension - very Pythonic:
```
squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]
evens = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
```
tips: Slicing never raises IndexError - it just returns what it can
List comprehensions are faster and more readable than loops
sorted(lst) returns a new list; lst.sort() sorts in-place

entries.title: ✨ List Comprehensions - 5 lines → 1 line
entries.content:
List comprehensions are the Pythonic way to build lists from other iterables.

C vs Python comparison:
```
// C: square every element
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    arr[i] = arr[i] * arr[i];

# Python: one line ✨
squares = [x * x for x in arr]
```

With a filter (if clause):
```
evens   = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
vowels  = [c for c in "hello world" if c in "aeiou"]
```

Nested comprehension (transpose a matrix):
```
matrix    = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]
transpose = [[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(3)]
```

Dict comprehension:
```
word_len = {w: len(w) for w in ["cat", "elephant", "ox"]}
# {'cat': 3, 'elephant': 8, 'ox': 2}
```
tips: If the comprehension is longer than ~80 chars, just write a regular loop
Generator expressions use () instead of [] - they're lazy (memory-friendly)
sorted(), min(), max() all accept key= functions - pair with lambda

entries.title: 🎀 Decorators (@) - wrapping logic elegantly
tips: Always use @functools.wraps(fn) inside your wrapper to preserve metadata
Decorators stack: @b @a def f() → f = b(a(f))
Built-in decorators you'll see: @staticmethod, @classmethod, @property

entries.title: 🧙 Dunder Methods - magic under the hood
entries.content:
Dunder (double-underscore) methods let your class hook into Python's built-in syntax.

The essentials:
```
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):      # constructor
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __repr__(self):            # for developers: repr(obj)
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __str__(self):             # for users: str(obj) / print(obj)
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __add__(self, other):      # v1 + v2
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

    def __len__(self):             # len(v)
        return 2

    def __eq__(self, other):       # v1 == v2
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

v1 = Vector(1, 2)
v2 = Vector(3, 4)
print(v1 + v2)   # (4, 6)  - uses __str__
print(repr(v1))  # Vector(1, 2)  - uses __repr__
```
tips: __repr__ should ideally return something you could paste to recreate the object
__str__ is what print() uses; falls back to __repr__ if not defined
Other useful ones: __len__, __contains__ (in), __iter__, __getitem__ ([])

entries.title: 📦 Venv & Packages - pip vs pacman vs apt
entries.content:
On 42 school machines or your own Linux system, managing Python packages cleanly matters.

Create and use a virtual environment:
```
python3 -m venv .venv          # create venv in .venv/
source .venv/bin/activate      # activate (bash/zsh)
pip install requests           # installs into .venv only
pip freeze > requirements.txt  # save dependencies
deactivate                     # leave venv
```

Install from a requirements file:
```
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Package manager cheat sheet:
```
# Arch Linux
pacman -Ss python-requests   # search
sudo pacman -S python-requests

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt install python3-requests

# Fedora/RHEL
sudo dnf install python3-requests

# Any distro (inside venv!)
pip install requests
```
tips: At 42, always use venv - you don't have sudo on the exam machines
Never pip install globally as root - it can break system Python packages
python3 -m pip is safer than bare pip if you have multiple Python versions

entries.title: ⌨️ Stdin / Stdout - sys.stdin & argparse
entries.content:
Two main ways to get input: command-line arguments or stdin.

sys.argv - raw arguments list:
```
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 3:
    print("Usage: prog arg1 arg2", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)

first  = sys.argv[1]
second = sys.argv[2]
```

argparse - proper argument parsing:
```
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="My tool")
parser.add_argument("name",            help="your name")
parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
args = parser.parse_args()

print(f"Hello {args.name}")
if args.verbose:
    print("verbose mode on")
```

Reading stdin line by line (pipe-friendly):
```
import sys
for line in sys.stdin:
    line = line.rstrip("\n")
    print(line[::-1])  # reverse each line
```

Print to stderr:
```
print("error!", file=sys.stderr)
```
tips: sys.argv[0] is always the script name - your args start at index 1
Use sys.exit(1) to signal failure to the shell (non-zero exit code)
argparse auto-generates --help for free!

entries.title: 🗂️ Dictionaries
entries.content:
Dicts store key-value pairs.

```
d = {"name": "alice", "age": 20}
d["age"]          # 20
d["city"] = "Lisbon"  # add a key
d.get("missing", 0)   # returns 0 instead of KeyError

# Iterate
for key, value in d.items():
    print(key, value)

# Check membership
if "name" in d:
    print("has name")
```
tips: Use .get() with a default to avoid KeyError
dict.keys(), dict.values(), dict.items() all return views
Dicts maintain insertion order since Python 3.7

entries.title: 🛠️ Functions & lambda
entries.content:
Functions are defined with def.

```
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Alice"))            # Hello, Alice!
print(greet("Bob", "Hey"))       # Hey, Bob!
```

Variable args:
```
def add(*args):            # tuple of positional args
    return sum(args)

def info(**kwargs):         # dict of keyword args
    for k, v in kwargs.items():
        print(k, v)
```

Lambda (anonymous function):
```
double = lambda x: x * 2
double(5)  # 10

# Common use: as a sort key
words = ["banana", "fig", "apple"]
words.sort(key=lambda w: len(w))  # sort by length
```
tips: Default arguments are evaluated once at definition - avoid mutable defaults like []
Return without a value returns None
Use *args and **kwargs for flexible function signatures

entries.title: 📖 OOP - Classes and Dunder Methods
entries.content:
Python uses classes to define objects.

```
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name, sound):
        self.name = name       # instance attribute
        self.sound = sound

    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} says {self.sound}"

dog = Animal("Dog", "woof")
print(dog.speak())   # Dog says woof
```

Inheritance:
```
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name):
        super().__init__(name, "woof")  # call parent __init__

    def fetch(self):
        return f"{self.name} fetches the ball!"

rex = Dog("Rex")
print(rex.speak())   # Rex says woof
print(rex.fetch())   # Rex fetches the ball!
```
tips: self is always the first parameter of instance methods
__init__ is the constructor - called when you create an object
super() lets you call the parent class's methods
